reference.source: OMIM / GeneReviews (NCBI) and standard clinical immunology texts
clinicalPearls: A form of leaky combined immunodeficiency, most often caused by hypomorphic variants in RAG1 or RAG2 that permit limited, oligoclonal T-cell development
Presents in early infancy with an erythrodermic, often exfoliative rash, alopecia and loss of eyebrows and eyelashes
Generalised lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly accompany failure to thrive and chronic diarrhoea
Characteristic laboratory picture is an elevated eosinophil count and markedly raised IgE with low or absent other immunoglobulins
T cells are present but restricted (oligoclonal) and activated, whereas B cells are typically absent or very low
The autologous activated T cells infiltrate skin, gut and other organs, producing a picture that can mimic graft-versus-host disease
Susceptibility to opportunistic and severe infection is high and the condition is fatal without treatment
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the definitive treatment, with immunosuppression to control the inflammatory phenotype beforehand
reference.pathophysiology: Omenn syndrome arises when residual (hypomorphic) activity of the V(D)J recombination machinery, most commonly RAG1 or RAG2, allows a small number of autoreactive T-cell clones to develop rather than complete arrest of lymphocyte maturation. Defective central and peripheral tolerance, thymic dysfunction and reduced regulatory T cells permit these oligoclonal, activated, T-helper-2-skewed T cells to expand and infiltrate the skin and gut, generating the erythroderma, eosinophilia and raised IgE. B-cell development fails, causing agammaglobulinaemia and profound infection susceptibility.
additionalDifferentials: Classic severe combined immunodeficiency without the Omenn phenotype
Maternal T-cell engraftment in severe combined immunodeficiency
Atopic dermatitis or other neonatal erythrodermas
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count with differential showing eosinophilia
Immunoglobulin levels demonstrating raised IgE with low IgG, IgA and IgM
Lymphocyte subset analysis and T-cell receptor repertoire (clonality) studies
Molecular genetic testing of RAG1, RAG2 and other combined immunodeficiency genes
Newborn screening T-cell receptor excision circle (TREC) assay where available
Skin biopsy and infection screen for opportunistic pathogens
redFlags: Severe or opportunistic infection in an infant with erythroderma
Rapidly worsening exfoliative rash with fluid and protein loss
Signs of end-organ infiltration or systemic inflammatory decompensation
Failure to thrive with intractable diarrhoea
reference.prognosis: Omenn syndrome is uniformly fatal in infancy without treatment. Timely haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, ideally after control of the inflammatory phenotype, offers the prospect of immune reconstitution and long-term survival.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the erythroderma as atopic dermatitis and delaying immunological evaluation
Overlooking the diagnosis because T cells are present, unlike classic severe combined immunodeficiency
Failing to consider maternal engraftment or graft-versus-host disease in the differential
Administering live vaccines or non-irradiated blood products before the immune defect is recognised
references: GeneReviews (NCBI): RAG deficiency and Omenn syndrome
